notes: All values are means over ALL consumer units in the group, including units that spent nothing on that line (e.g. rentedDwellings in the 'all' group averages renters and owners). Use the tenure groups for rent/owner comparisons.

BLS: 'Due to the 2025 lapse in federal appropriations, the Census Bureau could not collect the Consumer Expenditure Surveys (CE) ... in October and November 2025. BLS used a weight adjustment approach to account for these missing 2025 data.' (news release, 2026-10-29)

The 2025 calendar-year tables publish income before taxes only; no income-after-taxes or personal-taxes row is published, so incomeAfterTax is null. State tables publish personal taxes, stored as personalTaxes.

State groups are 2022-2023 two-year averages, which BLS calls a research product built with state research weights. BLS: 'As of May 2026, BLS will no longer produce state research products.' New Jersey's newest table (2019-2020) is omitted as too old.
MSA groups are 2023-2024 two-year averages, the newest available. BLS: it 'will not produce 2-year tabular estimates for 2024-2025' (variance-method change).

cpi.series: CUUR0000SA0 (CPI-U, US city average, all items, NSA)
cpi.note: October 2025 is missing ('Data unavailable due to the 2025 lapse in appropriations'); BLS states the 2025 annual average is calculated using 11 months of data.

Housing.note: Compare rent against the 'tenure-renter' group's rentedDwellings; a mortgage payment includes principal, which CE does not count as spending, so for owners compare only interest and property taxes, or show the CE figure as a lower bound.

Groceries.note: CE food at home is food only; grocery-store card charges also include non-food items (cleaning supplies, toiletries), so his figure will tend to run high.

Dining.note: CE food away from home includes meals on trips and school meals; alcohol is a separate CE line (alcohol) covering both home and away.

Gas & Auto.note: Excludes CE vehicle purchases (full net price recorded at purchase even when financed), vehicle finance charges and vehicle insurance (insurance maps to Insurance); loan payments in his ledger are not CE spending.

Travel.note: CE has no travel line: trip spending is split across other lodging (which also includes college housing and vacation homes), public transport (airfare plus local transit), food away and entertainment.

Shopping.note: CE has no 'shopping' line; merchant-based categorisation mixes apparel, household goods, electronics and gifts, so show these lines only as context.

Subscriptions & Digital.note: CE has no subscriptions line; streaming sits inside audio and visual equipment and services alongside TV and hardware, and phone/internet sit inside utilities.

Utilities & Bills.note: CE utilities include natural gas, electricity, fuel oil, telephone (incl. cellular) and water/public services; comparable if his phone and internet bills land in this category, and lower if utilities are included in rent.

Health.note: Compare only against the non-insurance lines; CE healthcare also includes health insurance premiums the household pays, which for most workers are payroll-deducted and never show up in his card or bank data.

Home.note: Home purchases split between Home and Shopping depending on the merchant, and CE household operations include childcare and other services he may not have; treat this as context only.

Entertainment.note: Compare only to CE fees and admissions (events, movies, sports, memberships); CE entertainment as a whole also includes pets, toys, audio/visual equipment and streaming.

Personal Care.note: CE personal care products and services covers hair, cosmetics, toiletries and salon services; drugstore toiletries may land in his Groceries or Shopping instead.

Insurance.note: Health premiums are usually payroll-deducted, homeowners insurance is buried inside an owned-dwellings line, and renters insurance has no separate line, so the total cannot be matched; vehicle insurance alone can be compared if he pays it directly.

Education.note: Means are over all households, most of which spend little or nothing, and tuition is lumpy, so compare annual totals only.

Gifts & Donations.note: CE cash contributions cover cash given to people and organisations outside the household; gifts bought as goods are recorded under the item's own category, not here.

Fees & Interest.note: CE records bank service charges inside Miscellaneous and vehicle/mortgage interest elsewhere; there is no line matching card interest and fees, so use the credit-card guideline instead.

Other.note: Uncategorised spending has no CE counterpart.

guidelines.label: 50/30/20: needs
guidelines.rule: Spend roughly 50% of after-tax income on needs.
guidelines.quote: This method allocates roughly 50% of your after-tax income to needs, 30% to wants, and 20% to savings or debt reduction.

guidelines.label: 50/30/20: wants
guidelines.rule: Spend roughly 30% of after-tax income on wants.
guidelines.metric: sum(non-needs spending categories) / monthly take-home pay
guidelines.quote: This method allocates roughly 50% of your after-tax income to needs, 30% to wants, and 20% to savings or debt reduction.

guidelines.label: 50/30/20: savings and debt reduction
guidelines.rule: Put roughly 20% of after-tax income toward savings or paying down debt.
guidelines.quote: This method allocates roughly 50% of your after-tax income to needs, 30% to wants, and 20% to savings or debt reduction.

guidelines.label: Housing cost burden (HUD)
guidelines.rule: A household is cost-burdened when housing costs, including utilities, exceed 30% of income.
guidelines.source: HUD Office of Policy Development and Research (CHAS)
guidelines.quote: Cost burden – Monthly housing costs (including utilities) exceeding 30% of monthly income.

guidelines.label: Severe housing cost burden (HUD)
guidelines.rule: A household is severely cost-burdened when housing costs, including utilities, exceed 50% of income.
guidelines.source: HUD Office of Policy Development and Research (CHAS)
guidelines.quote: Severe cost burden – Monthly housing costs (including utilities) exceeding 50% of monthly income.

guidelines.label: Mortgage debt-to-income (front-end)
guidelines.rule: Homeowners: keep mortgage principal and interest at 28-35% of gross monthly income or less.
guidelines.metric: mortgage principal + interest / gross monthly income
guidelines.quote: Consider maintaining a mortgage debt-to-income ratio of 28 to 35 percent.

guidelines.label: Total debt-to-income, homeowners (back-end)
guidelines.rule: Homeowners: keep all monthly debt payments, mortgage included, at 36% of gross monthly income or less.
guidelines.metric: all monthly debt payments incl. mortgage / gross monthly income
guidelines.quote: Consider maintaining a debt-to-income ratio for all debts of 36 percent or less. Some lenders will go up to 43 percent or higher. Your home mortgage is included in this ratio.

guidelines.label: Debt-to-income, renters
guidelines.rule: Renters: keep non-rent monthly debt payments at 15-20% of gross monthly income or less.
guidelines.metric: monthly debt payments excluding rent / gross monthly income
guidelines.quote: Consider maintaining a debt-to-income ratio for all debts of 15-20 percent or less. Your rent is not included in this ratio.

guidelines.label: Emergency fund
guidelines.rule: Keep three to six months of expenses in emergency savings; the right amount depends on income, expenses and household size.
guidelines.metric: liquid emergency savings / average monthly spending (months of coverage)
guidelines.quote: A general recommendation is to try to keep three to six months’ worth of expenses in your emergency savings fund.

otherSources.quote: Financial planners often recommend the equivalent of three to six months of living expenses, though those with variable income or specialized careers might need a larger reserve than those with stable jobs.
The amount you need to have in an emergency savings fund depends on your situation.

guidelines.label: Retirement savings rate
guidelines.rule: Save at least 15% of pre-tax income each year for retirement, counting any employer match.
guidelines.metric: (employee + employer retirement contributions) / gross annual income
guidelines.quote: we suggest aiming to save at least 15% of your pre-tax income each year, which includes any employer match.

guidelines.label: Pay credit cards in full
guidelines.rule: Paying the full statement balance by the due date each month keeps the grace period and avoids interest on purchases.
guidelines.metric: credit card interest charged (Fees & Interest), should be 0
guidelines.quote: If your card gives a grace period and you are not carrying a balance, then you can avoid paying interest on new purchases if you pay your balance in full by the due date.

countries.unit: percent of household final consumption expenditure (sum of COICOP divisions 01-12, domestic concept, current prices, national currency)
countries.dataset: OECD, Annual household final consumption expenditure by purpose (COICOP), DSD_NAMAIN10@DF_TABLE5_T501 v1.0
countries.presentation: share-of-total fun facts only; not comparable to a personal out-of-pocket ledger
caveats: National-accounts basis: includes imputed rent for owner-occupiers and spending paid on households' behalf, which is not in a card/bank ledger.
Domestic concept ('on the territory'): includes spending by foreign visitors and excludes residents' spending abroad; shares are computed over the 12 COICOP divisions.

2022 is the latest year with all 12 divisions for all 16 countries listed; 2023+ coverage is incomplete. Shares, not per-capita PPP dollars: levels would need separate PPP and population series and would still not be comparable.
